posts.body_html: After thinking about what bogman said about slimy peat and pulling air through the media/aeration, I was watching some of Mike King's youtube channel and wondering if anyone had given a peat-free mix a shot in the U.S. I know Mark Rienke uses crushed granite as his primary media and he doesn't seem to have any issue, although his bog has moving, fresh water from a creek to keep things flowing. I was considering testing out his peat-free mix, which he claims performs better than traditional. The mix I was planning was two parts crushed granite (he uses cornish grit), two parts pine bark nuggets and one part perlite.

After thinking about what bogman said about slimy peat and pulling air through the media/aeration, I was watching some of Mike King's youtube channel and wondering if anyone had given a peat-free mix a shot in the U.S. I know Mark Rienke uses crushed granite as his primary media and he doesn't seem to have any issue, although his bog has moving, fresh water from a creek to keep things flowing. I was considering testing out his peat-free mix, which he claims performs better than traditional. The mix I was planning was two parts crushed granite (he uses cornish grit), two parts pine bark nuggets and one part perlite.



At my old job where we grew Sarracenia commercially (yes, I once grew these plants on a very large scale), we trialed around 24 different soil and soiless media for potted Sarracenia plants in a 1/4 acre greenhouse (~20,000 plants total). Everything was grown in the same greenhouse (same environmental conditions), but watering was calibrated based on the type of media used. Results were measured in leaf mass produced within a 6 month period. the types of soil and soil mixes included almost everything you can imagine, as we ordered everything that was available or seemed reasonable to grow carnivorous plants in.

In terms of plant performance, nothing beat plain old 100% peat moss. I remember hearing parts of Europe banned the use of peat, which is probably why Mike King was forced to find an alternative or stop growing. Peat consumption is certainly problematic long term as it's not a sustainable medium, and the biggest threat to peat bogs is for the production of energy, followed by horticultural use.

In my opinion, The environmental cost of consuming a relatively small amount of peat to grow Sarracenia is exponentially outweighed by benefit of saving genotypes from long term extinction. Our consumption of peat is extremely efficient: I have community tubs of Sarracenia that haven't been transplanted in 9 years! Needless to say, many of us are getting as much "mileage" out of this precious, unrenewable resource as possible.

The trouble is, peat is being used to grow almost everything, which isn't good because many other crops can be grown in a less expensive, equally well performing soil mix. Fortunately, it seems Peat isn't being widely used as fuel here in the US, but if commercial growers continue to use peat over a renewable compost, it's only a matter of time when peat will be banned here in the US.

posts.body_html:
I think the challenge with pure sand or perlite+peat tea isn't maintaining the proper moisture content, but rather the lack of buffering capacity of the medium. pure peat is pretty darn resilient to a change in pH over time, but fine sand/perlite have a very poor buffering capacity (ie. ability to maintain a low pH level in this case). The tea alone will have a weak buffering capacity over time because there's relatively less organic material in it to buffer the pH. At first, You'll have a lot of free floating hydronium ions in peat tea, but once they're neutralized, there's nothing to "replace" them and keep the pH low...unless you're constantly renewing the peat tea. Root growth/water uptake from the plant can change the pH of a soiless medium. Nevertheless, it still seems worth testing, as theoretical results don't always equate to actual results!

The wild isn't as linear and crystal clear as it is in cultivation: it's likely in constant flux, so it's hard to say that what appears to be pure sand doesn't have other factors affecting it (ie. frequent rain, organic soil beneath or nearby, or a humic acid rich "tea" leaching into it slowly or frequently, micro-fauna activity, etc).

posts.body_html:
Like calen, I live on Oregon. I am located 100 miles South of him in the Willamette Valley.I have hundred of pots of Sarracenia - they all sit year around in kiddie pools with standing water from about 2 inches to about 4 inches deep, depending on how level the pool is. The pools are crowded with little or no space between pots. I bottom water as needed using RO water and never let the pools go dry. I have pot sizes varying from 4 inch to 12+ inches. In the same pools are dozens of pots of Flytraps and sundews.

I am pretty lazy about changing the media, generally only doing so when I divide a plant - usually when a pot is bulging badly. The media is 50:50 peat/perlite.

The pool water gets changed only by the fall/winter/spring rains, when there is overflow through the drainage holes in the sides of the pools.

I rarely have any rot problems.

I think next year I need to set up two identical pools, watering one as normal and the other only after the pool has been dry for a day or so. I can then see if plants perform better in one than in the other.

posts.body_html:
I just had to cut a huge chunk out of my HCW Clone F due to rot. I've been going through each plant for a mealybug inspection and cleanup and noticed a soft brown spot on the top of the HCW, uh oh. Started digging/cutting it away and it went all the way through to the bottom, lost 1.5" of rhizome to rot, about half of its mass. The only good news is that after I dug it up there was a decent size growth point under the peat that was trying to grow up into the original rhizome. Was able to make three small divisions out of what was left.

I replaced the tray it was in a couple months ago, the tray it was in for the last year had a crack in the side that wouldn't let it hold a full load of water. Low and behold, after switching to a tray that could hold 3", I got rot. I'm going back to a drained tray system for my leucos.
